title: Arafah and Ashura
hookLine: two voluntary fasts that expiate sins of past years (Muslim)
last: A DAY ON, A DAY OFF.

lines: NEAR THE START, NEAR THE END.
cards: Someone once asked the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ about fasting on two particular days of the year. His answers are kept in Sahih Muslim, and they reach a long way.
Fasting one of them, he said, wipes away the sins of the year before and the year after. Fasting the other wipes away the sins of the year before. Neither is required.
Both are remembered. One sits near the start of the Islamic year, the other near its end.

teach.h: ARAFAH: THE NINTH OF DHUL HIJJAH.
teach.b: First, Arafah: the ninth of Dhul Hijjah, the month of pilgrimage, the day the pilgrims stand on the plain of Arafah near Mecca, in prayer until sunset.

Muslims who aren't on pilgrimage can join that day from home by fasting it; that's the fast the hadith in Muslim ties to the year before and the year after. Second, a surprise: the pilgrims themselves aren't fasting.
In Sahih al-Bukhari, people at Arafah weren't sure whether the Prophet was fasting that day.
Umm al-Fadl sent him a cup of milk, and he drank it in front of everyone, standing there. The standing is the pilgrim's work that day; the fast belongs to those at home.
Third, Ashura, the tenth of Muharram, the first month.

teach.h: ASHURA: THE DAY MUSA WAS SAVED.
teach.b: A report in Bukhari says that when the Prophet came to Medina, he found the Jews of the city fasting that day, and they told him it was the day God saved Musa, Moses, and his people.

He fasted it and told the Muslims to fast it. A report in Muslim adds that late in his life he said, if he lived to the next year, he would fast the ninth as well. So some Sunni Muslims fast the ninth and tenth together.

teach.h: KARBALA, AND A DAY OF MOURNING.
teach.b: Tradition remembers it as the day of Karbala, where Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, was killed with his family and companions.
Shia communities keep Ashura above all as a day of mourning for Husayn, with gatherings, recitations and grief, and Shia scholars have their own rulings on fasting it.
The same day, held two ways, each with its reasons: a people saved, and a grandson lost.

how: Some Sunni Muslims fast the day of Arafah when not on pilgrimage, and fast Ashura with the day before it; for Shia Muslims, Ashura is a day of mourning for Husayn, marked with gatherings, and their scholars give their own rulings on fasting.

o: two voluntary single-day fasts of the Islamic year
the first and last nights of Ramadan's prayers
the two Eid festivals that close Ramadan and Hajj

games.q: Arafah and Ashura — tap the pairs.

s: pilgrims standing at Arafah are meant to be fasting
the Prophet drank milk at Arafah in front of everyone. the fast is for those at home.
the Arafah fast is tied to two years, the one before and the one after
so says the hadith in Sahih Muslim.
Ashura is kept the same way by every Muslim
some Sunni Muslims fast it; for Shia Muslims it is above all a day of mourning for Husayn.

games.q: you're with the Prophet at Arafah. people are arguing about whether he's fasting. Umm al-Fadl sends a cup of milk. what does he do?
o: drinks it, in front of everyone.
games.why: he drinks it where everyone can see. the question is settled: the pilgrim at Arafah isn't fasting.

practice: Choose one of the two days in your mind. If you're Muslim and you fast, picture the morning of that fast, what you'd eat before dawn, who you'd tell.
If not, picture what you might do that day to remember what it holds, a pilgrim's standing, or a family's grief.

wordCard.voice: Arafah and Ashura. The ninth of Dhul Hijjah and the tenth of Muharram, two voluntary fasts, each tied in Sahih Muslim to the wiping away of a year's sins. Today's word.

orig.note: the name of the tenth day of Muharram.

carryVoice: Your line: two special fasts. One near the year's end, one near its start. See you tomorrow.
